content: Pain in neonates is associated with immediate behavioral and physiological changes. Repeated exposure to pain can lead to long-term complications, including negative effects on neurodevelopment. Research has demonstrated that administering analgesics before painful procedures can reduce physiological changes and pain scores in neonates. Both non-pharmacological methods (such as holding, swaddling, and breastfeeding) and pharmacological methods (such as acetaminophen, sucrose, and opioids) have been employed to manage pain in this population. This review updates previous versions published in 2006 and 2012. The primary aim of this review was to assess the effectiveness of breastfeeding or supplemental breast milk in alleviating procedural pain in neonates. A secondary aim was to analyze subgroups based on the type of control intervention, gestational age, and the volume of supplemental breast milk provided. The search strategy included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, as well as trial registries like ICTRP, ISRCTN, and clinicaltrials.gov. The search was conducted in August 2022 and was limited to studies published from 2011 onward. Reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also examined. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs comparing breastfeeding or supplemental breast milk to no treatment or other interventions in neonates. Both term infants (≥37 weeks postmenstrual age) and preterm infants (<37 weeks postmenstrual age) up to 44 weeks postmenstrual age were included. Eligible studies reported on either physiological pain markers or validated pain scores. The methodological quality of the included trials was assessed using information from the studies and direct communication with the authors. Data on relevant outcomes were extracted, and effect sizes were calculated as mean differences (MD). The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. A total of 66 studies were included in the review. Of these, 36 studies evaluated breastfeeding, 29 studies assessed supplemental breast milk, and one study directly compared the two interventions. The procedures examined included heel lance (39 studies), venipuncture (11 studies), intramuscular vaccination (9 studies), eye examinations for retinopathy of prematurity (4 studies), suctioning (4 studies), and adhesive tape removal (1 study). There was significant variability in the control interventions and pain assessment methods used across the studies. Due to this heterogeneity, it was not possible to synthesize all interventions together. Instead, individual interventions were compared to breastfeeding or supplemental breast milk, and the findings were reported separately. Most studies were at low risk of bias, except for issues related to masking of interventions and outcome assessments, where nearly one-third of studies had a high risk of bias. Breastfeeding versus control: Breastfeeding may reduce the increase in heart rate compared to holding by the mother, skin-to-skin contact, bottle feeding with mother's milk, and moderate concentrations of sucrose/glucose (20%-33%) combined with skin-to-skin contact (low-certainty evidence, 8 studies, 784 participants). Breastfeeding likely reduces the duration of crying compared to no intervention, lying on a table, rocking, heel warming, holding by the mother, skin-to-skin contact, bottle feeding with mother's milk, and moderate concentrations of glucose (moderate-certainty evidence, 16 studies, 1866 participants). Breastfeeding may reduce the percentage of time spent crying compared to holding by the mother, skin-to-skin contact, bottle feeding with mother's milk, moderate concentrations of sucrose, and moderate concentrations of sucrose combined with skin-to-skin contact (low-certainty evidence, 4 studies, 359 participants). Breastfeeding likely reduces the Neonatal Infant Pain Scale (NIPS) score compared to no intervention, holding by the mother, heel warming, music, EMLA cream, moderate glucose concentration, swaddling, and swaddling combined with holding (moderate-certainty evidence, 12 studies, 1432 participants). Breastfeeding may reduce the Neonatal Facial Coding System (NFCS) score compared to no intervention, holding, pacifier use, and moderate concentrations of glucose (low-certainty evidence, 2 studies, 235 participants). Breastfeeding may reduce the Douleur Aiguë Nouveau-né (DAN) score compared to positioning, holding, or placebo (low-certainty evidence, 4 studies, 709 participants). In most other comparisons, there was little or no difference between breastfeeding and the control group in any of the outcome measures. Supplemental breast milk versus control: Supplemental breast milk may reduce the increase in heart rate compared to water or no intervention (low-certainty evidence, 5 studies, 336 participants). Supplemental breast milk likely reduces the duration of crying compared to positioning, massage, or placebo (moderate-certainty evidence, 11 studies, 1283 participants). Supplemental breast milk results in little or no difference in the percentage of time spent crying compared to placebo or glycine (low-certainty evidence, 1 study, 70 participants). Supplemental breast milk results in little or no difference in NIPS scores compared to no intervention, pacifier use, moderate concentrations of sucrose, eye drops, gentle touch and verbal comfort, or breast milk odor combined with verbal comfort (low-certainty evidence, 3 studies, 291 participants). Supplemental breast milk may reduce NFCS scores compared to glycine (low-certainty evidence, 1 study, 40 participants). DAN scores were lower when compared to massage and water, showed no difference when compared to no intervention, EMLA cream, or moderate concentrations of sucrose, and were higher when compared to rocking or pacifier use (low-certainty evidence, 2 studies, 224 participants). Due to the large number of comparator interventions, other pain measures were assessed in only a small number of studies, resulting in low-certainty evidence. Most studies did not report adverse events, likely due to the benign nature of the interventions. Those that did report adverse events found none among participants. Subgroup analyses were not conducted because of the limited number of studies. Conclusions: Moderateto low-certainty evidence suggests that breastfeeding or supplemental breast milk may reduce pain in neonates undergoing painful procedures compared to no intervention, positioning, holding, placebo, or other non-pharmacological interventions. Low-certainty evidence indicates that moderate concentrations of glucose or sucrose (20%-33%) may have little or no difference in pain reduction compared to breastfeeding. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of breast milk for painful procedures in preterm neonates, as current evidence in this population is limited.
